name: leasehound
description: 🐕 Sniffs out the lease clauses that shouldn't be there — WA tenant-law RAG: clause-by-clause scan reports with statute citations, grounded Q&A, and an evaluation-driven retrieval pipeline

paragraphs: Upload your lease. LeaseHound sniffs out the clauses that shouldn't be there. A two-layer RAG system that answers tenant-law questions and scans rental agreements for prohibited provisions — grounded in Washington State's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (RCW 59.18).

🐕 Live demo — one click scans the sample lease, warm and answering in 100 ms (how that stays free) · live API docs — the same pipeline as a typed contract, because the UI is one client of three, not the product.

LeaseHound 🐕 — you hand it a document; it examines what is in front of it. RentScout 🐕‍🦺 — you send it out; it decides where to look and comes back with a report. One is a workflow. The other is an agent. Building both is the point.

whatItDoes.text: Upload your lease. LeaseHound sniffs out the clauses that shouldn't be there. A two-layer RAG system that answers tenant-law questions and scans rental agreements for prohibited provisions — grounded in Washington State's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (RCW 59.18).

requirements.text: A caller needs the counts early to size a progress bar, and split fires before the gate so that costs nothing — but a caller that promises something from those counts has promised it before anything decided the scan would happen.

COPY vectordb shipped the whole development store — the three ablation collections the evaluation needs and the app never queries, including 230split, an experiment that was measured and rejected. scripts/exportruntimedb.py now writes a purpose-built store holding only the collection the app serves; it costs nothing, because every chunk's embedding already exists and is copied…
It needs no API key and nothing beyond the standard library, so it costs $0 whether or not the law changed.
